name: Thymus
func: A gland behind the sternum (chest bone) where T cells, a key type of white blood cell, are trained. It teaches them to attack germs but not your own body. It is largest in childhood and shrinks into fat in adults.

levels.kid:
The **thymus** is a soft gland in your chest, sitting right behind the flat bone in the middle and just above your **heart**.

It is like a **school for soldiers**. Your body has special fighter cells called **T cells** that protect you from germs. Baby T cells come to the thymus to learn.

In the thymus, they take tests. They learn to spot bad **germs**, and they learn **not** to hurt your own body. Only the T cells that pass the tests get to graduate and go out to protect you.

The thymus is biggest and busiest when you are a kid, then it slowly shrinks when you grow up.
levels.hs:
The **thymus** is a primary **lymphoid organ**, which means it is a place where immune cells are made and trained, not just where they gather. It sits in the **superior** and **anterior mediastinum**, the space in the middle of the chest, **behind the sternum** (the flat chest bone) and in front of the **great vessels** of the heart (the aorta, the pulmonary trunk and the left brachiocephalic vein) and the upper **pericardium**. It has two lobes and may extend up into the neck toward the thyroid.

Its job is to produce mature **T lymphocytes** (the "T" stands for thymus). Immature cells travel from the **bone marrow** to the thymus, where they learn to:
1. **Recognize** foreign invaders when shown pieces of them on the body's own **MHC** molecules.
2. **Ignore** the body's own tissues, so they do not cause **autoimmune** disease.

Most of the trainee cells, well over 90%, fail and die. The survivors become **helper T cells (CD4)** or **killer T cells (CD8)**.

The thymus is relatively large in babies and children and keeps growing until the early teens. After that, it gradually undergoes **involution**: it is replaced by fat. Adults still have a little active thymic tissue, but they rely mostly on T cells made earlier in life.
levels.college:
**Development**: the thymus arises from the **third pharyngeal pouch** (endoderm), along with the inferior parathyroid glands, and migrates down into the chest. Missing or ectopic thymic tissue reflects this path.

**Structure**: a fibrous capsule sends septa inward, dividing each lobe into **lobules** with an outer **cortex** and inner **medulla**.
- The **cortex** is packed with immature **thymocytes** and **cortical thymic epithelial cells (cTECs)**.
- The **medulla** has fewer, more mature thymocytes, **medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs)**, **dendritic cells** and **Hassall's corpuscles**, concentric whorls of keratinized epithelial cells.

**T-cell development** follows a path from cortex to medulla: progenitors enter at the **corticomedullary junction**, become **double-negative** (CD4−CD8−), rearrange their **T-cell receptor** genes, then become **double-positive** (CD4+CD8+). In the cortex, **positive selection** keeps cells whose receptors can bind self-MHC weakly; the rest die by neglect. In the medulla, **negative selection** deletes cells that bind self-antigens too strongly. Cells end up single-positive CD4 (if they bound MHC class II) or CD8 (MHC class I).

The **blood–thymus barrier** in the cortex, formed by endothelium, pericytes and epithelial cells, limits antigen entry during selection.

**Blood supply**: from the **internal thoracic arteries** and inferior thyroid arteries; veins drain mainly into the **left brachiocephalic vein**. On imaging, a child's thymus can look large and sail-shaped (the **thymic sail sign**) and should not be mistaken for a mass.
levels.phd:
**Central tolerance** depends on mTECs expressing thousands of tissue-restricted antigens, such as insulin and proteins normally found only in specific organs, a phenomenon called **promiscuous gene expression**. The transcriptional regulator **AIRE** (autoimmune regulator) drives much of this. **AIRE** mutations cause **APECED** (autoimmune polyendocrinopathy–candidiasis–ectodermal dystrophy), in which autoreactive T cells attack the adrenals, parathyroids and other organs. **FEZF2** controls another set of tissue antigens independently of AIRE.

Recent work has shown that some mTECs adopt the identities of other cell types, so-called **mimetic cells** (muscle-like, gut-like, skin-like, neuroendocrine), each showing tissue-specific proteins to developing T cells (Mathis and colleagues).

Selection depends on **TCR signal strength**: weak signals rescue cells (positive selection), and strong signals cause deletion or diversion into **regulatory T cells (Tregs)**, which express **FOXP3** and prevent autoimmunity. FOXP3 mutations cause **IPEX** syndrome. cTECs express a unique proteasome subunit (**β5t**, the thymoproteasome) that generates special peptides for positive selection.

The thymic epithelium itself depends on the transcription factor **FOXN1**; its loss causes the "**nude**" phenotype in mice (no hair, no thymus) and severe immunodeficiency in humans. **DiGeorge syndrome** (22q11.2 deletion, including TBX1) disrupts pharyngeal pouch development, causing thymic and parathyroid hypoplasia and heart defects.

**Thymic involution** reduces T-cell output with age, contributing to weaker responses to new infections and vaccines in older adults. It is driven by changes in the epithelium, fat accumulation and hormonal and inflammatory signals; regeneration (via IL-22, BMP4, KGF) is being researched, especially after chemotherapy and bone marrow transplant.
levels.expert:
**Myasthenia gravis** is the key clinical link. It is an autoimmune disease in which antibodies, most often against **acetylcholine receptors**, block nerve-to-muscle signaling, causing **fatigable weakness**: drooping eyelids, double vision, trouble chewing and swallowing, and in severe cases **respiratory failure** (myasthenic crisis). About 10–15% of patients have a **thymoma**, and many others have **thymic hyperplasia** with germinal centers. **CT of the chest** is done in every new diagnosis.

**Thymectomy** improves outcomes in generalized, antibody-positive myasthenia even without a thymoma, as shown by the **MGTX randomized trial**. It can be done through a **median sternotomy** or minimally invasive approaches (video-assisted or robotic). Protecting the **phrenic nerves**, which run along the sides of the gland, is essential.

**Anterior mediastinal masses**: the classic "**4 Ts**" are **thymoma**, **teratoma** (germ cell tumors), **thyroid** (retrosternal goiter) and "terrible" **lymphoma**. Thymomas are staged by the **Masaoka–Koga** system and classified by the WHO; **thymic carcinoma** is more aggressive. Large anterior mediastinal masses can collapse the airway or compress the heart during anesthesia, a serious risk for surgeons and anesthetists.

**Immunodeficiency**: absent thymic function (complete **DiGeorge syndrome**) causes severe T-cell deficiency and infections; it is treated with **thymus tissue implantation**. Newborn screening for **severe combined immunodeficiency** measures **TRECs** (T-cell receptor excision circles), a marker of new T cells leaving the thymus.

In children, the normal thymus can look large on chest X-ray (**sail sign**) and shrink during illness or stress, then rebound.

keyPoints: Sits in the anterior/superior mediastinum behind the sternum, in front of the great vessels
Trains T cells: positive selection in the cortex, negative selection in the medulla
Largest in childhood, then involutes and is replaced by fat
AIRE in medullary epithelial cells shows self-antigens to enforce tolerance
Linked to myasthenia gravis; thymoma is a top anterior mediastinal mass

test.q: The thymus develops from which embryonic structure?
test.explain: The third pharyngeal pouch also forms the inferior parathyroid glands.

test.q: Where does negative selection of self-reactive T cells mainly happen?
test.explain: Medullary epithelial cells, guided by AIRE, show self-antigens and delete strongly self-reactive cells.

test.q: The autoimmune disease of fatigable weakness linked to the thymus is myasthenia ______.
test.explain: Many patients have thymic hyperplasia or a thymoma; thymectomy can help.

test.q: Which gene lets thymic cells show proteins from other organs?
test.explain: AIRE drives promiscuous gene expression; its mutation causes APECED.

test.q: The shrinking of the thymus with age is called thymic ______.
test.explain: Thymic tissue is gradually replaced by fat, lowering new T-cell output.
